match.reason: No point in the bank covers floating versus fixed exchange rate systems; the closest ones, the balance of payments and net trade, only touch on currency effects, so this needs a new point.

draft.title: Floating and fixed exchange rates
card: the exchange rate is set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market. Australia floated the dollar in December 1983, and the Reserve Bank (RBA) does not set its value.
the government or central bank sets the rate against another currency or a basket of currencies. The central bank must buy or sell currency to hold the rate in place.
A floating rate adjusts on its own. If export prices fall, demand for the dollar falls and the dollar depreciates, which can cushion the economy by making exports cheaper abroad.
To defend a fixed rate, the central bank may use its reserves of foreign currency or change interest rates. If reserves run low, it may be forced to change the rate.
draft.remember: A floating rate moves with the market. A fixed rate must be defended by the central bank.

a.q: Which statement best describes how the Australian dollar's value is set today?
opts: By supply and demand in the foreign exchange market
By the RBA, which sets a target rate each year
By the Treasurer, who announces the rate each month
By a fixed link to the US dollar
a.why: Australia floated the dollar in 1983, so market supply and demand set its value. The RBA can trade in the market, but it does not set a fixed rate, which is why the RBA option is wrong.

b.q: Country X fixes its currency to the US dollar. Investors start selling X's currency and demand for it falls. What must X's central bank do to keep the rate fixed?
opts: Buy its own currency using foreign currency reserves
Sell its own currency to push the rate down
Let the rate fall until demand recovers
Stop trading in the foreign exchange market
b.why: To hold a fixed rate when demand falls, the central bank must buy its own currency, using its foreign currency reserves. Letting the rate fall is what a floating system does, so it would end the fix.
b.clue: The central bank must make up for the fall in demand.

a.best: By supply and demand in the foreign exchange market

b.best: Buy its own currency using foreign currency reserves

proposal.title: Floating and fixed exchange rates
card: the exchange rate is set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market. Australia floated the dollar in December 1983, and the Reserve Bank (RBA) does not set its value.
the government or central bank sets the rate against another currency or a basket of currencies. The central bank must buy or sell currency to hold the rate in place.
A floating rate adjusts on its own. If export prices fall, demand for the dollar falls and the dollar depreciates, which can cushion the economy by making exports cheaper abroad.
If demand for a fixed currency falls, the central bank can buy its own currency with its foreign currency reserves, or raise interest rates. If reserves run low, it may be forced to change the rate.
proposal.remember: A floating rate moves with the market. A fixed rate must be defended by the central bank.

a.q: Which feature belongs to a fixed exchange rate but not a floating one?
opts: The central bank trades currency to hold the rate in place
Supply and demand alone set the value of the currency
The rate adjusts on its own when export prices fall
The rate can cushion the economy when a shock hits
a.why: Under a fixed rate, the central bank has to buy or sell currency to stop the rate moving. Adjusting on its own and cushioning shocks are features of a floating rate, where supply and demand set the value.
a.clue: Which system needs someone to defend the rate?
